sections.text:
We must now turn to our opponents and refute the objections brought against us from “knowledge falsely so called.” They say that the Holy Spirit must not be ranked together with the Father and the Son because his nature is different and his dignity inferior. It is right to answer them in the words of the apostles: “We must obey God rather than human beings.”

For if the Lord, when handing down saving baptism, clearly commanded the disciples to baptize all nations into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, not disdaining the Spirit's fellowship with himself, while these men say that the Spirit must not be ranked with Father and Son, how are they not plainly resisting God's command?

If they say that such coordination does not indicate fellowship or union, let them tell us what they think it does indicate and what closer form of union they can propose. If the Lord did not join the Spirit with himself and the Father in baptism, then they should not accuse us of joining them, for we think and say nothing other than what is written. But if the Spirit is there joined with Father and Son—and no one is so shameless as to say otherwise—then they must not accuse us when we follow Scripture.

Yet the whole preparation for war against us has been made ready; every intellectual weapon is aimed at us, and blaspheming tongues shoot at us more violently than the stones once thrown at Stephen. They should not conceal from themselves that the attack on us is merely the pretext: the real assault is aimed higher.

They claim to build their engines and lay their traps against us, each urging the others on according to his skill or strength. But what is being attacked is the faith. The common aim of all the opponents and enemies of sound teaching is to shake the foundation of faith in Christ by leveling apostolic tradition to the ground and destroying it.

Therefore, like supposedly conscientious debtors, they demand written proofs while dismissing the unwritten testimony of the fathers as worthless. But we shall not retreat from the truth or betray its defense through cowardice.

The Lord handed down to us, as a necessary and saving teaching, the ranking of the Holy Spirit with the Father. Our opponents think otherwise: they divide and separate him and transfer him into the nature of a ministering spirit. Do they not thereby make their own blasphemy more authoritative than the legislation of the Master?

Come, then: setting aside contentiousness, let us consider the matters before us together.

From where are we Christians? Through faith, everyone would answer. And in what way are we saved? Plainly by being born again through the grace of baptism. How else?

Having recognized that this salvation is established through Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, shall we cast away the form of teaching that we received? Would it not deserve great lamentation if we were now found farther from our salvation than when we first believed, denying now what we confessed then?

Whether someone leaves this life without baptism or receives a baptism lacking something belonging to the handed-down form, the loss is grave. Whoever does not preserve at every time and throughout life, as a secure safeguard, the confession made at the first entrance—when, being turned away from idols, we approached the living God—makes himself a stranger to God's promises and fights against his own signed confession of faith.

If baptism was for me the beginning of life, and the day of regeneration the first of days, then plainly the confession uttered in the grace of adoption was most honorable of all. Shall I now, led astray by persuasive arguments, betray the tradition that introduced me into light, gave me knowledge of God, and through which I, once an enemy because of sin, became a child of God?

For myself I pray to depart to the Lord with this confession. I exhort others to preserve the faith inviolate until the day of Christ and to keep the Spirit inseparable from Father and Son, maintaining in both confession of faith and completion of the doxology the teaching received at baptism.

translator_notes: Direct Mercy translation from Basil's Greek PG 32 text.
This chapter grounds the Spirit's coordination with Father and Son in the baptismal command of Matthew 28:19.
Basil distinguishes written scriptural proof from the apostolic/patristic tradition embodied in baptismal confession and doxology.
